name: English
areas: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts

short.Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and respo: U1 Reading and responding to t

source: Adapted revision checklist based on VCAA's VCE English and EAL Study Design, Units 3 and 4. Checkpoints are skills-based because set texts and Frameworks of Ideas differ between schools; apply each checkpoint to your own texts. Checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs, not VCAA numbering.
practiceNote: These practice questions and marking guides are original revision exercises, not VCAA examination questions. Because your set texts differ, most questions ask you to apply a skill to a text you are studying rather than testing recall of a particular book.
papers: The examination has three sections: analytical interpretation of a text, creating texts, and analysis of argument. Use the VCAA examination specifications, past examinations and examination reports for official assessment resources.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Understanding the whole text
points.detail: Knowing plot, structure, setting and the arc of each major character well enough to select evidence from anywhere in the text without rereading it.

questions.q: Explain why a detailed knowledge of a text's structure, not just its plot, improves an analytical response.
answer: Structure includes how the text is divided, the order in which information is revealed and where shifts in perspective or time occur.
Knowing structure lets you argue about the effect of authorial choices, such as why a revelation is withheld until the final chapter.
A response that only retells plot describes what happens, whereas analysis of structure explains how the author shapes the reader's response.

card.title: Understanding the whole text
back: Knowing plot, structure, setting and the arc of each major character well enough to select evidence from anywhere in the text without rereading it.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Authorial intent and construction
points.detail: Treating the text as something deliberately made, and writing about the author's choices rather than about characters as if they were real people.

questions.q: Rewrite the following in a way that shows the text is constructed: 'Macbeth becomes paranoid because he feels guilty about the murder.'
answer: A constructed version: 'Shakespeare charts Macbeth's descent into paranoia to dramatise the corrosive effect of guilt on the conscience.'
The subject of the sentence becomes the author, and the verb names a deliberate choice such as charts, positions, constructs or undercuts.
This shifts the response from describing a person to analysing an authorial decision and its effect on the audience.

card.title: Authorial intent and construction
back: Treating the text as something deliberately made, and writing about the author's choices rather than about characters as if they were real people.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Views and values
points.detail: Identifying what a text endorses, challenges or leaves ambiguous, and locating the textual evidence that reveals it.

questions.q: Explain how you would establish, with evidence, what a text values, and state one common error students make.
answer: Look at which characters or behaviours are rewarded and which are punished by the narrative's outcome.
Look at the language used to describe them, since sympathetic or unsympathetic diction reveals the text's judgement.
Consider what the text leaves unsaid or unresolved, as ambiguity may itself be the position being taken.
A common error is assuming a character's views are the author's views; the author may present a view in order to criticise it.

card.title: Views and values
back: Identifying what a text endorses, challenges or leaves ambiguous, and locating the textual evidence that reveals it.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Unpacking the prompt
points.detail: Identifying the key terms, the assumption embedded in the prompt and the scope it sets, before planning any argument.

questions.q: Outline the steps in unpacking an essay prompt before you begin planning.
answer: Identify the key words and define any that are contestable, since the definition often becomes part of your argument.
Identify the assumption the prompt makes and decide whether you agree with it fully, partly or not at all.
Note the scope: whether the prompt limits you to a character, a theme, a section of the text or the whole text.
Decide your contention, which should answer the prompt directly rather than restate it.

card.title: Unpacking the prompt
back: Identifying the key terms, the assumption embedded in the prompt and the scope it sets, before planning any argument.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Types of prompts
points.detail: Recognising theme-based, character-based, quotation and 'how' prompts, and adapting the approach each requires.

questions.q: Explain how your approach differs between a prompt beginning 'To what extent' and one beginning 'How does the author'.
answer: A 'to what extent' prompt invites a qualified position, so the essay should concede part of the statement before arguing the more significant qualification.
A 'how does the author' prompt is asking about method, so each paragraph must be organised around a technique or choice and its effect.
In both cases the contention must take a clear position rather than sitting on the fence.

card.title: Types of prompts
back: Recognising theme-based, character-based, quotation and 'how' prompts, and adapting the approach each requires.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Writing a contention
points.detail: Stating a single, arguable position that responds to the prompt and previews the line of reasoning the essay will follow.

questions.q: Explain what separates a strong contention from a weak one, and give an example of each in general terms.
answer: A weak contention restates the prompt or lists the paragraph topics without taking a position.
A strong contention makes a claim that could be disagreed with, and signals the reasoning that supports it.
It should also be specific to the text, referring to the author's purpose rather than making a general observation about life.

card.title: Writing a contention
back: Stating a single, arguable position that responds to the prompt and previews the line of reasoning the essay will follow.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Introductions
points.detail: Opening with the text and author, establishing the contention, and signalling the argument without listing paragraph topics mechanically.

questions.q: State what an effective text response introduction must contain and one thing it should avoid.
answer: It must name the text, its form and the author, and state the contention in response to the prompt.
It should signal the line of reasoning, so the reader knows the direction the argument will take.
It should avoid broad opening generalisations about human nature and avoid mechanically listing 'firstly, secondly, thirdly'.

card.title: Introductions
back: Opening with the text and author, establishing the contention, and signalling the argument without listing paragraph topics mechanically.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Topic sentences and paragraph structure
points.detail: Opening each paragraph with a claim that advances the contention, then supporting it with evidence and analysis before linking back.

questions.q: Explain the function of a topic sentence and describe a reliable paragraph structure for a text response.
answer: The topic sentence states the argument of the paragraph, not the events it will discuss, and it must advance the contention.
Follow it with evidence: a brief embedded quotation or a precise reference to a moment in the text.
Analyse the evidence by explaining the author's choice and its effect on the reader, rather than paraphrasing the quotation.
Close by linking the point back to the contention so the argument accumulates rather than restarting each paragraph.

card.title: Topic sentences and paragraph structure
back: Opening each paragraph with a claim that advances the contention, then supporting it with evidence and analysis before linking back.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Embedding evidence
points.detail: Integrating short quotations into your own sentences so they read fluently, and selecting the most precise words rather than long passages.

questions.q: Explain why short embedded quotations are usually more effective than long block quotations in a text response.
answer: A short embedded quotation lets you analyse specific word choices, which is where the analysis actually happens.
Long quotations consume words without demonstrating your reasoning, and the marker cannot tell which part you consider significant.
Embedding also keeps the sentence grammatical and shows control of the material rather than reliance on it.

card.title: Embedding evidence
back: Integrating short quotations into your own sentences so they read fluently, and selecting the most precise words rather than long passages.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Analysing language and technique
points.detail: Moving from identifying a technique to explaining its effect, and using precise metalanguage appropriate to the text's form.

questions.q: Explain the difference between identifying a technique and analysing it, and give the structure of an analytical sentence.
answer: Identifying names the device, for example noting that the author uses a simile, which earns little credit on its own.
Analysing explains what the choice does: the connotation it carries, the response it creates and how it serves the author's purpose.
A useful structure is: the author's choice, the specific evidence, the connotation or effect, and the link to purpose or theme.

card.title: Analysing language and technique
back: Moving from identifying a technique to explaining its effect, and using precise metalanguage appropriate to the text's form.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Metalanguage for prose
points.detail: Narrative perspective, focalisation, free indirect discourse, tone, imagery, motif, symbolism, characterisation and structure in novels and short fiction.

questions.q: Explain the effect of a first person unreliable narrator and name the metalanguage you would use to discuss it.
answer: A first person narrator restricts the reader to one character's perspective, so the reader receives only that character's interpretation of events.
Unreliability creates a gap between what the narrator claims and what the reader infers, which can generate irony or invite judgement.
Useful terms include narrative perspective, focalisation, dramatic irony, retrospective narration and free indirect discourse.

card.title: Metalanguage for prose
back: Narrative perspective, focalisation, free indirect discourse, tone, imagery, motif, symbolism, characterisation and structure in novels and short fiction.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Metalanguage for drama
points.detail: Stage directions, dramatic irony, soliloquy and aside, staging, lighting and sound, act and scene structure, and the audience rather than the reader.

questions.q: Explain why a response to a play should refer to the audience rather than the reader, and name two dramatic techniques worth analysing.
answer: A play is written to be performed, so meaning is produced through staging, performance and the shared experience of an audience.
Soliloquy grants the audience privileged access to a character's interior thought, creating intimacy or complicity.
Dramatic irony, where the audience knows what a character does not, generates tension and invites judgement of that character.

card.title: Metalanguage for drama
back: Stage directions, dramatic irony, soliloquy and aside, staging, lighting and sound, act and scene structure, and the audience rather than the reader.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Metalanguage for film
points.detail: Mise en scene, framing and shot type, camera movement, editing, lighting, colour palette, sound and score, and the term viewer rather than reader.

questions.q: Name four film techniques and briefly state a typical effect of each.
answer: A close-up isolates a face or object, directing attention to emotion or significance.
A low angle shot positions the viewer beneath the subject, conveying power, dominance or threat.
Non-diegetic score guides emotional response by cueing the viewer how to feel about the action on screen.
Editing pace, such as rapid cutting, builds tension, while a long take can create unease or intimacy.

card.title: Metalanguage for film
back: Mise en scene, framing and shot type, camera movement, editing, lighting, colour palette, sound and score, and the term viewer rather than reader.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Metalanguage for poetry and memoir
points.detail: Form, stanza and line break, enjambment, metre and rhythm, voice, persona, and the conventions of life writing.

questions.q: Explain the effect of enjambment and why the distinction between poet and persona matters.
answer: Enjambment runs a sentence across a line break, creating momentum, hesitation or a moment of double meaning at the line's end.
The persona is the voice constructed within the poem and is not necessarily the poet themselves.
Maintaining the distinction allows you to analyse voice as a deliberate construction rather than as autobiography.

card.title: Metalanguage for poetry and memoir
back: Form, stanza and line break, enjambment, metre and rhythm, voice, persona, and the conventions of life writing.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Context and its limits
points.detail: Using historical, social and cultural context to illuminate the text's concerns, without letting background information displace textual analysis.

questions.q: Explain how context should be used in a text response and the most common way students misuse it.
answer: Context should be used briefly to explain why a concern mattered to the author or original audience, sharpening the analysis.
It must be connected immediately to a specific choice in the text rather than presented as standalone background.
The common misuse is a paragraph of historical information with no textual evidence, which reads as a history answer rather than an English one.

card.title: Context and its limits
back: Using historical, social and cultural context to illuminate the text's concerns, without letting background information displace textual analysis.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Complexity and counter-argument
points.detail: Acknowledging tension, ambiguity or counter-evidence in the text, and using it to produce a more nuanced position rather than a contradictory one.

questions.q: Explain how to handle evidence that appears to contradict your contention.
answer: Acknowledge it directly rather than ignoring it, since ignoring obvious counter-evidence weakens the argument.
Show why the apparent contradiction is consistent with a more precise version of your contention, for example that the text is ambivalent rather than wholly endorsing.
Use qualifying language such as 'while', 'although' and 'ultimately' to hold both ideas at once.
The strongest responses treat tension in the text as the subject of analysis rather than a problem to be hidden.

card.title: Complexity and counter-argument
back: Acknowledging tension, ambiguity or counter-evidence in the text, and using it to produce a more nuanced position rather than a contradictory one.

points.area: Units 3 and 4 — AoS 1: Reading and responding to texts
points.title: Conclusions
points.detail: Drawing the argument together, extending to the text's broader significance, and avoiding both mere repetition and the introduction of new evidence.

questions.q: State what an effective conclusion does and two things it should not do.
answer: It should restate the position in language different from the introduction and draw the strands of the argument together.
It may extend briefly to the text's wider significance or to what the author invites the audience to consider.
It should not introduce new evidence or a new argument, and it should not simply repeat the introduction word for word.

card.title: Conclusions
back: Drawing the argument together, extending to the text's broader significance, and avoiding both mere repetition and the introduction of new evidence.

points.title: The Framework of Ideas
points.detail: Understanding the chosen Framework as a field of ideas to explore, and generating your own angle within it rather than writing to a fixed topic.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of a Framework of Ideas in Creating texts and how it differs from an essay topic.
answer: The Framework provides a broad field of ideas that your writing explores, such as writing about country, protest, personal journeys or play.
It is not a question to answer; you develop your own angle, argument or narrative within that field.
The Framework sets the territory, while your purpose, audience, context and form are decisions you make.

card.title: The Framework of Ideas
back: Understanding the chosen Framework as a field of ideas to explore, and generating your own angle within it rather than writing to a fixed topic.

points.title: Purpose, audience, context and form
points.detail: Making deliberate decisions about why you are writing, for whom, in what circumstances and in what form, and keeping them consistent across the piece.

questions.q: Explain how a decision about audience changes the writing that follows, using two specific features as examples.
answer: Audience determines register: a piece for a specialist readership can assume shared knowledge, while a general audience needs explanation.
It determines the level of formality in vocabulary and syntax, including whether contractions, slang or first person are appropriate.
It determines what evidence or appeal will be persuasive, since different readers respond to different kinds of authority.
Inconsistency in these features is one of the clearest signals that a writer has not held their audience in mind.

card.title: Purpose, audience, context and form
back: Making deliberate decisions about why you are writing, for whom, in what circumstances and in what form, and keeping them consistent across the piece.

points.title: Learning from mentor texts
points.detail: Reading mentor texts as a writer, identifying the specific moves they make, and adapting those moves rather than imitating their content.

questions.q: Explain what it means to read a mentor text 'as a writer' and give two features worth borrowing.
answer: Reading as a writer means noticing how the piece is built rather than only what it says, identifying choices you could reuse.
Structural moves are worth borrowing, such as opening with a concrete image before widening to an idea.
Voice features are also worth borrowing, such as the rhythm of short sentences after a long one, or a recurring motif that ties the piece together.

card.title: Learning from mentor texts
back: Reading mentor texts as a writer, identifying the specific moves they make, and adapting those moves rather than imitating their content.

points.title: Voice and register
points.detail: Constructing a consistent and deliberate voice through diction, syntax, rhythm and distance, and sustaining it across the whole piece.

questions.q: Name three elements that create voice in a piece of writing and explain how one of them can be varied for effect.
answer: Voice is created through word choice, sentence length and rhythm, and the degree of distance or intimacy with the reader.
Sentence length can be varied deliberately: a sequence of longer sentences followed by a short one gives that short sentence weight.
Consistency matters, because an unexplained shift in voice reads as a loss of control rather than a deliberate effect.

card.title: Voice and register
back: Constructing a consistent and deliberate voice through diction, syntax, rhythm and distance, and sustaining it across the whole piece.

points.title: Structure in creative and persuasive writing
points.detail: Choosing a shape that serves the purpose: linear, fragmented, circular, framed or vignette, and controlling the reader's experience of time and revelation.

questions.q: Explain one non-linear structure and the effect it can achieve.
answer: A circular structure returns at the end to the image or moment that opened the piece.
The repetition invites the reader to reinterpret that opening in light of everything that has followed, producing a sense of change or of inescapability.
The structure itself carries meaning, so the choice should be justified by the piece's purpose rather than used for novelty.

card.title: Structure in creative and persuasive writing
card.front: Structure in creative and persuasive writing
back: Choosing a shape that serves the purpose: linear, fragmented, circular, framed or vignette, and controlling the reader's experience of time and revelation.

points.title: Showing rather than telling
points.detail: Conveying emotion and meaning through concrete detail, action and image rather than through abstract statement.

questions.q: Explain the principle of showing rather than telling and why it is more effective.
answer: Telling states a feeling directly, for example that a character was nervous, which gives the reader a label but no experience.
Showing presents concrete detail from which the reader infers the feeling, such as an action, a physical sensation or a fragment of dialogue.
It is more effective because inference engages the reader in making meaning, and specific detail is more memorable than abstraction.

card.title: Showing rather than telling
back: Conveying emotion and meaning through concrete detail, action and image rather than through abstract statement.

points.title: Vocabulary and precision
points.detail: Choosing words for connotation as well as denotation, avoiding vague abstractions and resisting the impulse to inflate vocabulary artificially.

questions.q: Explain why the most impressive vocabulary is not always the most effective, and state the test to apply.
answer: A word used for its impressiveness rather than its precision often carries connotations the writer did not intend.
Overly elevated diction can also clash with the voice and register established elsewhere in the piece.
The test is whether the word is the most precise available for the meaning intended, not whether it is the least common.

card.title: Vocabulary and precision
back: Choosing words for connotation as well as denotation, avoiding vague abstractions and resisting the impulse to inflate vocabulary artificially.

points.title: Experimentation and risk
points.detail: Trying unfamiliar forms, perspectives and structures during the writing process, and judging which experiments serve the purpose.

questions.q: Explain the value of experimenting with form during Creating texts and how to judge whether an experiment has worked.
answer: Experimentation develops range and often produces a more distinctive piece than the first, most obvious approach.
An experiment works when the unusual choice does something the conventional choice could not, such as a second person address creating complicity.
It fails when the reader's attention goes to the technique itself rather than to the meaning it was meant to create.

card.title: Experimentation and risk
back: Trying unfamiliar forms, perspectives and structures during the writing process, and judging which experiments serve the purpose.

points.title: Drafting, feedback and editing
points.detail: Treating writing as a process of drafting and revision, using feedback critically, and editing at the level of structure before the level of the sentence.

questions.q: Explain why structural editing should come before sentence-level editing.
answer: Structural editing decides what stays, what is cut and in what order material appears.
Polishing a sentence that will later be deleted wastes effort, so large decisions should be made first.
Once the shape is settled, sentence-level editing can sharpen word choice, rhythm and clarity within it.

card.title: Drafting, feedback and editing
back: Treating writing as a process of drafting and revision, using feedback critically, and editing at the level of structure before the level of the sentence.

points.title: The written commentary or reflection
points.detail: Explaining the decisions made about purpose, audience, context, form and language, and justifying them with reference to your own text and your mentor texts.

questions.q: State what a written commentary on your own writing should contain.
answer: An explicit statement of the intended purpose, audience, context and form of the piece.
Identification of specific choices you made in language, structure and voice, quoted or referenced from your own writing.
A justification of why each choice serves the purpose and audience you identified.
Acknowledgement of the mentor texts or Framework ideas that influenced the decisions, and of what you changed between drafts.

card.title: The written commentary or reflection
back: Explaining the decisions made about purpose, audience, context, form and language, and justifying them with reference to your own text and your mentor texts.

points.title: Identifying contention and arguments
points.detail: Distinguishing the overall contention from the supporting arguments, and tracking how the arguments develop across the text.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a contention and an argument, and how to identify each in an opinion piece.
answer: The contention is the writer's overall position, the single claim the whole piece exists to persuade the reader to accept.
Arguments are the separate reasons offered in support, usually one per section or paragraph.
The contention is often stated near the opening or the close, while arguments can be found by asking what each paragraph is trying to prove.

card.title: Identifying contention and arguments
back: Distinguishing the overall contention from the supporting arguments, and tracking how the arguments develop across the text.

points.title: Audience, context and purpose
points.detail: Identifying the intended audience and the issue's context, and considering what that audience already believes and what the writer needs to shift.

questions.q: Explain why identifying the intended audience improves an analysis of argument.
answer: Persuasive effect depends on the reader: an appeal to tradition may reassure one audience and alienate another.
Knowing the audience lets you explain why the writer chose a particular appeal rather than simply naming it.
It also explains structural choices, such as conceding a point early to disarm readers who are likely to disagree.

card.title: Audience, context and purpose
back: Identifying the intended audience and the issue's context, and considering what that audience already believes and what the writer needs to shift.

points.title: Tone and its shifts
points.detail: Naming tone precisely, tracking where and why it changes, and linking the shift to the writer's persuasive strategy.

questions.q: Explain how to write about a shift in tone, and give three precise tone words that are more useful than 'negative'.
answer: Identify where the shift occurs, name both tones precisely, and explain what the change is designed to achieve.
A shift from measured to indignant, for example, can signal that the writer has moved from establishing credibility to demanding action.
Precise alternatives include derisive, wry, conciliatory, sardonic, urgent and resigned.
Vague labels such as 'negative' or 'emotive' do not explain how the reader is being positioned.

card.title: Tone and its shifts
back: Naming tone precisely, tracking where and why it changes, and linking the shift to the writer's persuasive strategy.

points.title: Appeals and persuasive strategies
points.detail: Appeals to fear, hip pocket nerve, family, patriotism, fairness, tradition and expertise, and the reasoning each invites the reader to accept.

questions.q: Explain how an appeal to fear positions a reader, and why naming the appeal alone earns few marks.
answer: An appeal to fear presents an undesirable consequence as likely if the reader does not accept the writer's position.
It positions the reader to feel personally at risk, making the writer's proposal seem like protection rather than imposition.
Naming the appeal alone is mere identification; the analysis is in explaining the specific reasoning and response it invites.
Strong responses explain what the reader is encouraged to conclude and why that conclusion serves the contention.

card.title: Appeals and persuasive strategies
back: Appeals to fear, hip pocket nerve, family, patriotism, fairness, tradition and expertise, and the reasoning each invites the reader to accept.

points.title: Language techniques in argument
points.detail: Inclusive language, rhetorical questions, repetition, anecdote, statistics, expert opinion, emotive diction, hyperbole and attacks, and the effect of each.

questions.q: Explain the persuasive effect of an anecdote and of statistics, and why a writer might use both.
answer: An anecdote makes an abstract issue concrete and personal, inviting the reader to feel sympathy for an individual case.
Statistics create an impression of objectivity and scale, suggesting the individual case is representative rather than exceptional.
Used together, the anecdote supplies emotional engagement while the statistics supply apparent proof.
The combination positions the reader to accept both that the issue matters and that it is widespread.

card.title: Language techniques in argument
back: Inclusive language, rhetorical questions, repetition, anecdote, statistics, expert opinion, emotive diction, hyperbole and attacks, and the effect of each.

points.title: Analysing visuals
points.detail: Reading photographs, cartoons, graphs and layout for their persuasive contribution, and connecting the visual to the written argument.

questions.q: Explain how to analyse a political cartoon and what must be included for full marks.
answer: Describe only the details that matter persuasively, such as exaggeration of a figure, symbolic objects, labels and facial expression.
Explain the contention the cartoon advances and how the visual choices position the viewer to accept it.
Explain the relationship to the written text: whether the visual reinforces, extends or complicates the writer's argument.
A description of the image without analysis of its effect earns very little credit.

card.title: Analysing visuals
back: Reading photographs, cartoons, graphs and layout for their persuasive contribution, and connecting the visual to the written argument.

points.title: Structuring an analysis of argument
points.detail: Organising the response by the movement of the argument rather than by a list of techniques, and maintaining a sustained line of analysis.

questions.q: Explain why structuring an analysis around the argument's development is better than structuring it around a list of techniques.
answer: A technique-by-technique structure produces a catalogue that repeats the same phrasing and loses sight of the writer's overall strategy.
Structuring by the development of the argument follows how the writer builds the case and shifts the reader over the course of the piece.
This allows you to explain sequence and cumulative effect, such as establishing credibility before making a contentious claim.
Techniques are then analysed where they occur, in service of the argument being made at that point.

card.title: Structuring an analysis of argument
back: Organising the response by the movement of the argument rather than by a list of techniques, and maintaining a sustained line of analysis.

points.title: Comparing two or more texts
points.detail: Analysing how different writers position readers on the same issue, and comparing strategy, tone and appeal rather than summarising each in turn.

questions.q: Explain how to compare two argument texts effectively.
answer: Compare the contentions first, noting whether they oppose each other or differ in emphasis or scope.
Compare the strategies used to position the reader, such as one writer relying on expertise while the other relies on personal experience.
Integrate the comparison within paragraphs using connectives such as 'whereas' and 'by contrast', rather than analysing one text then the other.
Account for differences in audience and form, since these often explain why the strategies differ.

card.title: Comparing two or more texts
back: Analysing how different writers position readers on the same issue, and comparing strategy, tone and appeal rather than summarising each in turn.

points.title: Metalanguage of analysis
points.detail: Using precise verbs for what a writer does to a reader, and avoiding the repeated formula of 'this makes the reader feel'.

questions.q: Give four precise verbs for describing what a writer does to a reader and explain why they are preferable to 'makes the reader feel'.
answer: Useful verbs include positions, invites, implies, aligns, undermines, concedes, dismisses and casts.
They describe the persuasive mechanism rather than asserting an emotional outcome the writer cannot guarantee.
'Makes the reader feel' overstates the effect and is usually followed by an unsupported claim about emotion rather than analysis of reasoning.

card.title: Metalanguage of analysis
back: Using precise verbs for what a writer does to a reader, and avoiding the repeated formula of 'this makes the reader feel'.

points.title: Sentence variety and control
points.detail: Varying sentence length and structure for rhythm and emphasis, and controlling complex sentences without losing clarity.

questions.q: Explain how sentence length can be used for emphasis and name one risk of long sentences.
answer: A short sentence placed after several longer ones lands with emphasis because of the contrast in rhythm.
Long sentences can accumulate detail and hold ideas in relation to one another, which suits complex analysis.
The risk is losing grammatical control, so that the subject and verb become separated and the meaning blurs.

card.title: Sentence variety and control
back: Varying sentence length and structure for rhythm and emphasis, and controlling complex sentences without losing clarity.

points.title: Cohesion and paragraph linking
points.detail: Using connectives, pronoun reference and repeated key terms to carry an argument forward without mechanical signposting.

questions.q: Name three ways to create cohesion between paragraphs and state one to avoid.
answer: Repeat or vary a key term from the previous paragraph in the opening of the next, so the thread is visible.
Use logical connectives such as 'consequently', 'by contrast' or 'more troublingly' that signal the relationship between ideas.
Build a sequence in which each paragraph complicates or extends the previous one rather than simply adding another example.
Avoid mechanical signposting such as 'the second point I will discuss is', which announces structure without creating it.

card.title: Cohesion and paragraph linking
back: Using connectives, pronoun reference and repeated key terms to carry an argument forward without mechanical signposting.

points.title: Concision
points.detail: Removing filler phrases, redundant qualifiers and empty openings so that every sentence carries meaning.

questions.q: Identify the problem in this sentence and rewrite it: 'It is important to note that the author uses a range of different techniques in order to show the reader that the character is very isolated.'
answer: The sentence opens with filler, uses redundant wording such as 'range of different' and 'in order to', and relies on the vague intensifier 'very'.
It also identifies techniques without naming any, so it makes no analytical claim.
A concise revision: 'The author's spare, fragmented syntax enacts the character's isolation.'

card.title: Concision
back: Removing filler phrases, redundant qualifiers and empty openings so that every sentence carries meaning.

points.title: Punctuation for meaning
points.detail: Using the colon, semicolon, dash and comma deliberately, and avoiding the comma splice and misplaced apostrophe.

questions.q: Explain the correct use of a semicolon and a colon, and identify what a comma splice is.
answer: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses that could each stand as a sentence.
A colon introduces an explanation, elaboration or list that follows from the clause before it.
A comma splice incorrectly joins two independent clauses with only a comma; it is repaired with a full stop, a semicolon or a conjunction.

card.title: Punctuation for meaning
back: Using the colon, semicolon, dash and comma deliberately, and avoiding the comma splice and misplaced apostrophe.

points.title: Titles, tenses and conventions
points.detail: Italicising or underlining titles correctly, writing about texts in the present tense, and using the author's surname after first full mention.

questions.q: State three conventions for writing about texts in English responses.
answer: Titles of novels, plays and films are italicised or underlined; titles of poems and short stories take quotation marks.
Write about events in a text in the present tense, since the text continues to do what it does on every reading.
Give the author's full name at first mention and the surname thereafter, and spell both the author's name and characters' names correctly.

card.title: Titles, tenses and conventions
back: Italicising or underlining titles correctly, writing about texts in the present tense, and using the author's surname after first full mention.

points.title: Using reading time
points.detail: Allocating reading time across the three sections, choosing the text and prompt, and beginning to plan mentally before writing is permitted.

questions.q: Describe how you would use the exam's reading time across the three sections.
answer: Go first to the section that requires a choice, locating your text and reading both prompts before deciding.
Read the argument material next, since it is unseen and takes the longest to absorb, noting contention and tone as you read.
Use the remaining time to begin forming a contention for the text response, so writing can begin immediately.

card.title: Using reading time
back: Allocating reading time across the three sections, choosing the text and prompt, and beginning to plan mentally before writing is permitted.

points.title: Timing and allocation
points.detail: Dividing writing time roughly evenly across the three sections, and starting the next section on time even if the current one feels unfinished.

questions.q: Explain why finishing all three sections matters more than perfecting one, in terms of marks.
answer: Each section is marked separately and carries the same weight, so an unwritten section scores zero.
The marks lost by leaving a section unattempted far exceed the marks gained by polishing a response that is already sound.
Moving on at the planned time, and returning later if time permits, protects the total score.

card.title: Timing and allocation
back: Dividing writing time roughly evenly across the three sections, and starting the next section on time even if the current one feels unfinished.

points.title: Planning under time pressure
points.detail: Producing a short plan that fixes the contention and the order of arguments, and knowing when planning has become procrastination.

questions.q: State what a useful exam plan contains and roughly how long it should take.
answer: A contention in one sentence, and three or four topic sentences or argument stubs in order.
Two or three pieces of specific evidence noted against the arguments they support.
It should take only a few minutes, since the purpose is direction rather than a draft.

card.title: Planning under time pressure
back: Producing a short plan that fixes the contention and the order of arguments, and knowing when planning has become procrastination.

points.title: Common examiner criticisms
points.detail: Retelling plot, listing techniques, generic introductions, ignoring part of the prompt and running out of time, and how to avoid each.

questions.q: Name four criticisms examiners commonly make of English responses and state how to avoid each.
answer: Retelling rather than analysing: fix by starting each paragraph with a claim rather than an event.
Listing techniques without effect: fix by following every identification with its effect and link to purpose.
Ignoring part of the prompt: fix by underlining the key terms and checking the plan addresses all of them.
Running out of time: fix by allocating time per section in advance and keeping to it.

card.title: Common examiner criticisms
back: Retelling plot, listing techniques, generic introductions, ignoring part of the prompt and running out of time, and how to avoid each.
